First 3 seconds: Rolling shot of a red lifted late-model Super Duty dually on the highway, edited so it sits on tiny stock-size wheels under the big lift; text sits above it the whole time; rap track playing
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "California Trucks When The Tire Ban Kicks In"
Why it went viral: 88x the account median but only 0.9% shares: a news-peg joke about a rule people were already angry about, and the wrong-looking truck reads in one glance, so it pulled reach and comment arguments more than sends. The politics did the distribution, not the truck.
Who sends it, to whom: Lifted truck owners to the buddy on 38s; out-of-state guys to their California friend as a jab
Shape you can borrow alone: One clip of your own truck plus one line of text tying it to a truck rule or price everyone is already arguing about this week.

Why it went viral: avoid: the laugh rides on a reaction clip of a real person who appears to have a disability, his face is the punchline. The share engine underneath (5.54% shares, 48x median) is the fuel price pain plus the red diesel wink, which is worth noting on its own.
Who sends it, to whom: Diesel owners to the buddy who jokes about running farm fuel

First 3 seconds: Same white OBS still and the same cutout reaction clip of a man taking a shot and grimacing; red text on top

Why it went viral: avoid: same reaction clip as bensdiesels-02, a real person who appears to have a disability used as the joke face. Proof the fuel price plus red diesel premise repeats (3.67% shares, 37x median) six months later with one line changed.
Who sends it, to whom: Diesel owners to the buddy who complains about the pump

First 3 seconds: Night shot of his white lifted OBS at a gas pump; cartoon Monsters Inc characters edited into the cab bouncing around; text above; movie line "Get out of the car, please" lands at 4 s
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When the homie and I are filling up and he starts messing with my 30 year old truck..."
Why it went viral: A 7 second loop on a feeling every old-truck owner has (do not touch anything, it is fragile), with a movie audio line as the punchline. 31x median and 2.79% shares because it names a specific friend.
Who sends it, to whom: Old truck owners to the friend who slams the door or plays with the switches
Shape you can borrow alone: One static shot of your truck, text naming a thing a passenger does that makes you nervous, and a known audio line as the punchline.

First 3 seconds: Black frame with white title text and a letterboxed 2 Fast 2 Furious phone call scene (the "you want to race tonight" call); original movie dialogue playing
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "If Brian O'Connor Drove A 7.3 Powerstroke (Accurate Edition)"; audio: "Yeah, man, you want a race tonight?"
Why it went viral: Movie recut with his OBS dropped in: glow plug wait, slow trip, then it loses power and misses the race. Self-roast of the 7.3 that owners agree with, plus 50 s of story, gave 4.7% shares at 27x median. "Accurate Edition" answers the comments on the earlier version, which pulls those people back.
Who sends it, to whom: 7.3 owners to each other and to the Cummins buddy who calls it slow; Fast and Furious fans
Shape you can borrow alone: Take a famous scene everybody knows and retell it with your truck's real flaws as the plot, told by you to camera or with your own truck shots as the cutaways.

First 3 seconds: Dark night scene, generated or CG: a white OBS drives up a huge curved ramp, launches off the top, then lands on rocket smoke; no on-screen text, the joke lives in the caption
Hook (said or on screen): Caption: "7.3 owners will literally learn to fly before buying a new truck"
Why it went viral: Absurd visual that holds the eye for 13 s, tied to a true identity line (7.3 guys never upgrade). 27x median, 3.14% shares. The "X owners will literally do Y before Z" sentence is the portable part.
Who sends it, to whom: 7.3 owners to each other; wives and buddies to the guy who will not sell his old truck
Shape you can borrow alone: One line in the form "[truck] owners will literally [absurd thing] before [sensible thing]" over a clip of you doing the absurd fix.

First 3 seconds: Door of the white OBS opens, he climbs in (legs and arm only, no face), then a close shot of his hand turning the key; red script text mid-screen
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "1997 7.3L Coldstart"
Why it went viral: Pure sound and ritual: key turn, exhaust tip close up, engine settling. 24x median but 0.36% shares, so it was watched and liked, not sent. Reach from sound-on replays in winter, nothing to pass to a friend.
Who sends it, to whom: Barely shared; 7.3 fans save or like it
Shape you can borrow alone: Three shots, no talking: get in, key turn, exhaust tip. Good filler for reach, weak for sends.

First 3 seconds: Drone orbit of the white OBS hooked to a fifth-wheel camper with a pontoon boat double-towed behind it in an empty lot; question text up, answer text pops in at 2 s
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "How much can a 7.3L tow?" then "All of it."
Why it went viral: Asks the question strangers always ask and answers in three words with a picture that proves it. 23x median, 3.06% shares, and the double tow starts a legal or not fight in the comments.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck guys to the buddy who says old trucks cannot work; campers and boat owners
Shape you can borrow alone: Put the question you get asked most on screen in quotes, answer it in three words, and let one wide shot of the truck doing it be the proof.

First 3 seconds: Black frame with a movie-poster title and a Tokyo Drift street scene where his white OBS is edited in place of Han's car with Han leaning on it; song from the film playing
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "F7.3 Not Fast, Very Furious"
Why it went viral: 7 second single-image joke: a title pun that roasts his own truck for being slow. 16x median, 3.64% shares. Short enough to loop twice, and the pun is the thing people forward.
Who sends it, to whom: 7.3 owners to each other; Fast and Furious fans to truck friends
Shape you can borrow alone: A movie-title pun about your truck's best-known weakness over one still or slow push-in of the truck.

First 3 seconds: Same black frame and 2 Fast 2 Furious phone call scene as bensdiesels-05, original dialogue; later his OBS with blue underglow leaves the garage and this time makes the race
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When 7.3 owners add a KC Turbo and Hydra"; audio: "Yeah, man, you want to race tonight?"
Why it went viral: Highest share rate of his ten (8.18%) at 14x median. Names two parts that every 7.3 owner either has or wants, so it flatters the guys who bought them and tags the brands; the movie scene carries the watch time.
Who sends it, to whom: 7.3 owners to the buddy who just did a turbo and tuner, and to the one still stock
Shape you can borrow alone: Name the two mods your crowd argues about and show the before and after attitude of the owner, played by you alone in the cab.

Who sends it, to whom: Girlfriends to boyfriends (caption bait); OBS fans to each other
Shape you can borrow alone: Slow continuous walkaround, tail to cab to interior, one caption line that tells a specific person to send it to another.

Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Why do you run ambers & 16" alcoas?" then script text "Old school"

Why it went viral: Fuel price before and after with a political soundbite underneath. 10x median but 0.1% shares, so the reach came from comment fights, not sends. Same lesson as bensdiesels-01: pump pain gets views, the political framing does not get forwarded.
Who sends it, to whom: Few; mostly argued over in comments

First 3 seconds: Handheld pan along the white OBS from the bed toward the cab at dusk while a voiceover joke starts; then he opens the door on a messy interior for the punchline
Hook (said or on screen): Audio: "I like my trucks like I like my women" ... "in the 90s, couple previous owners" ... "and all messed up on the inside"
Why it went viral: A trending joke audio where the reveal (opening the door on a trashed cab) lands right on the punchline. 10x median, 0.74% shares. The timing of door-open to the last line is the whole trick. The joke is at women's expense, so it is not one to copy as written.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck guys to buddies
Shape you can borrow alone: Voice sets up a comparison on the outside of the truck, the door opens on the punchline. Keep the roast aimed at yourself or the truck.

First 3 seconds: Handheld walk starting at the tailgate (FORD lettering, 4x4 decal) and moving up the driver side in daylight; no text, music only

Why it went viral: Plain daylight walkaround of a spotless crew cab long bed. 10x median, 0.57% shares. The truck itself is the content; nothing here that travels beyond people who already love OBS Fords.
Who sends it, to whom: OBS fans, lightly
Shape you can borrow alone: One-take walkaround of a clean truck. Works only when the truck is the star and pays in views, not sends.

Hook (said or on screen): Audio: "You think I'm psycho, don't you, mom?"; caption: "Obs ford period correct 40/20/40s in front and rear"

First 3 seconds: Low close shot at dusk on the front corner of the lifted white OBS, amber corner light on, camera drifting back along the fender to the cab; old trucker ballad playing, no text
Hook (said or on screen): Caption: "Clean and simple."; song opens "You heard about the legend of Jesse James"

Who sends it, to whom: Sons to dads, older truck guys to each other (the song does it)
Shape you can borrow alone: Slow dusk walkaround at a gas station cut to one old song your dad's generation knows.

Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Randy is quite the dump truck operator" (no speech)
Why it went viral: An absurdly overloaded old work truck plus a named guy and a dry one-line caption; it is a sight gag anyone gets in one second, which is why it pulled 48x the account median. Share rate is low (0.22%), so it spread on watch and likes more than sends.
Who sends it, to whom: Guys who work dirt or farm, to the coworker who always overloads the truck
Shape you can borrow alone: One continuous shot of a truck doing something visibly ridiculous at work, with a single deadpan caption naming the culprit.

First 3 seconds: Low handheld glide along the bed of a lifted blue and cream 1977 Ford highboy on big tires, parked in a metal carport
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Anyone want to buy it?" (no speech)
Why it went viral: A clean two-tone highboy is a dream truck for this crowd and the for-sale question turns every viewer into a buyer or a tagger. 1.23% shares on 846k views is the 'look what is for sale' send.
Who sends it, to whom: Dentside fans to the buddy or spouse they would need permission from
Shape you can borrow alone: Slow 15 second walkaround of one truck with a single question on screen that invites a yes or a tag.

Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Take your pick" (old-time country song under it)
Why it went viral: A row of five or six trucks and a forced choice; people answer in comments and send it to argue the pick. 1.85% shares and 28x median show the choose-one prompt doing the work.
Who sends it, to whom: Classic Ford guys to the friend they argue trucks with
Shape you can borrow alone: Walk past several trucks or parts in one take and ask the viewer to pick one.

Why it went viral: Pure eye candy: mirror black paint, chrome and swampers shot close and smooth with a nostalgic country song. Nothing to explain, just a truck people want, and 1.25% sent it.
Who sends it, to whom: Dentside owners to the friend building one, as a 'this is the goal' send

Hook (said or on screen): No text; George Strait "Ocean Front Property" playing
Why it went viral: Same recipe as his other hits: rare color combo, big tires, tight detail shots and a classic country track, then a reveal of more trucks in the room. 1.64% shares at 27x median.
Who sends it, to whom: Older Ford fans to a brother or dad who had one that color
Shape you can borrow alone: Start on a tight detail, pull back to reveal the whole truck and then the room it sits in.

Hook (said or on screen): No text; song lyric "like I'm a prisoner of the highway"
Why it went viral: First-person 'get in and start it' sequence: door opens on a mint red interior, key turns, gauges come alive. Viewers stay for the start-up payoff, though shares were low (0.19%) so it grew on watch time and likes.
Who sends it, to whom: Men who grew up riding in one, to a dad or brother (weakly; this one is watched more than sent)
Shape you can borrow alone: Point of view walk-up, open the door, sit, turn the key, end on the gauges.

Hook (said or on screen): Text: "What do you think think about this '72 powerstroke?" (typo in original; no speech)

Who sends it, to whom: Powerstroke and classic Ford guys to the purist friend who will hate it

Who sends it, to whom: Truck guys to friends with 'imagine having this barn'

Hook (said or on screen): No text; song lyric about a phone ringing
Why it went viral: Eleven seconds, three trucks, quick whip pans, loops easily. Same 'which one' pull as the collection clip with 2.51% shares.
Who sends it, to whom: Dentside fans to the buddy who shares their taste
Shape you can borrow alone: Very short clip that whips between two or three vehicles, built to loop.

Why it went viral: Shows the part most videos skip: a spotless underside with headers and red shocks on a nearly finished build, plus 'for sale soon' in the caption. Shares 0.57%, so interest was mostly watch and comment.
Who sends it, to whom: Builders to a friend mid-project, as a standard to hit
Shape you can borrow alone: Walkaround that goes under the truck or behind a panel to show the work nobody normally films.

Why it went viral: A well known monster truck story clip laid over calm, pretty shots of an old mud-tire Ford; the audio is the hook and the truck fits the 'old junk' line. 146x the account median with 0.8% shares, so the borrowed story carried it.
Who sends it, to whom: Monster truck and OBS fans to buddies who know the Grave Digger story
Shape you can borrow alone: Lay a short spoken story (your own voice) over four or five locked-off beauty shots of the truck.

First 3 seconds: Night shot of the lifted OBS with one front tire climbed up on a parking lot curb, axle flexed, cab lights on
Hook (said or on screen): Audio: "Wow, Kristie. Do you see that truck? ... That is so tacky. That must be one of those rednecks I've heard about."
Why it went viral: Self-deprecating: he plays the snobby voice that judges his truck and answers with the truck flexing and rolling down the road. Owners of loud lifted trucks see themselves, and 1.4% sent it at 106x median.
Who sends it, to whom: Lifted truck owners to each other and to the wife or friend who calls the truck tacky
Shape you can borrow alone: Quote what critics say about your truck, then answer with nothing but footage of the truck being exactly that.

First 3 seconds: Same sunset hay stack location, wide shot of the OBS side-on, cuts to it framed between two hay walls
Hook (said or on screen): No text; rap song lyric "I guess it was meant to be" (caption: Thoughts on the 14 wides?)
Why it went viral: Good light, a striking location and a single opinion question in the caption about a divisive tire choice. 98x median but only 0.7% shares, so comments and rewatch drove it.
Who sends it, to whom: OBS guys to the friend deciding on tires
Shape you can borrow alone: Three or four still tripod shots at golden hour with one opinion question about a single part.

First 3 seconds: Rear view of the OBS on wet pavement reflecting the sky, big swampers, quoted text at top
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Bro why would you get swampers they ride like sht" then "..." over a roller of the truck (audio is a borrowed TV-style voice clip)
Why it went viral: Answers a real complaint with no defense at all: quote the critic, then just show the truck rolling on the tires looking great. Every mud tire owner has heard the line. Highest share rate for this account in the set (2.58%).
Who sends it, to whom: Guys on swampers or mud tires to the buddy who gives them grief for the ride
Shape you can borrow alone: Put the criticism on screen as a quote, then cut to a wordless shot of the truck that is the whole answer.

First 3 seconds: Locked-off silhouette of the OBS on a road against a blazing orange sunset over a green field
Hook (said or on screen): No text; song lyric "started with hello darling" (caption: First and second clip)
Why it went viral: Just very good pictures: three sunset compositions of the same truck with a slow song. The caption nudges a rewatch to compare clips; 0.94% shares.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck people to a friend as a wallpaper-type send
Shape you can borrow alone: Three locked-off sunset shots of the truck, ask which clip is best.

First 3 seconds: Foggy frosted hillside, OBS small in frame with lights on, then a close low shot of the front tire and brush guard
Hook (said or on screen): Audio: "I absolutely hated it. I thought it was the most grandpa farm-looking truck ever..." (caption: Brushgaurd?)
Why it went viral: Uses a borrowed 'I hated it at first' voice clip to frame a new brush guard, then asks for a verdict. A relatable change-of-mind beat on one part; 1.12% shares at 65x median.
Who sends it, to whom: OBS owners to friends debating the same add-on
Shape you can borrow alone: Admit you hated a part or look at first, show it on the truck, ask for the verdict.

Hook (said or on screen): No speech, no text
Why it went viral: Lightning behind a lit-up lifted truck is a rare shot and the storm does all the work in 14 seconds. 50x median, 1.0% shares; mostly a 'look at this' clip.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck and storm people to friends, as a cool shot

First 3 seconds: Bright day, OBS driving slowly toward camera on a gravel road between wheat fields under big clouds
Hook (said or on screen): Text and audio: "How many mpg does that thing get?" ... "0.8" at the gas pump ... "Well that's not economical at all" ... "Nope!"
Why it went viral: The single most asked question of any lifted gas truck, answered with a joke number and a cut to the pump, in nine seconds. Everyone with a thirsty truck relates; 0.72% shares.
Who sends it, to whom: Gas truck owners to whoever keeps asking about their mileage
Shape you can borrow alone: Put the question you get asked most on screen, answer with one cutaway shot and a one-word reply.

First 3 seconds: Close side shot of the front fender and huge tire at dusk, pink horizon behind
Hook (said or on screen): Song lyric as caption and audio: "Just an old half ton short bed Ford"
Why it went viral: The lyric literally describes the truck, so the song and the picture click, and it taps dad and uncle nostalgia. 41x median, 1.15% shares.
Who sends it, to whom: Men to their dad or uncle, or anyone who learned to drive in an old Ford
Shape you can borrow alone: Pick a song line that literally describes the truck and cut plain detail shots to it.

First 3 seconds: Sunset hay stack wide shot again with text over it
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Sure you can look at what I reposted... but if you want to know how I actually feel, look at what I have saved,"
Why it went viral: A general trend text pasted over reused truck footage; it has nothing to do with trucks and people did not send it (0.22% shares). Views likely came from the trend and the pretty footage. Weakest model of the ten.
Who sends it, to whom: Unclear; few people shared it
Shape you can borrow alone: Not much to borrow; if anything, a personal one-line thought over still truck shots.

First 3 seconds: Tom leans out the window of a white 65 Mustang, then a greasy hand flips three red toggle switches (FP, FAN, ACC) and turns a key with an 8-ball keychain
Hook (said or on screen): No words until the end; after the tach jumps and the side exhaust barks he asks "Better?"
Why it went viral: The start-up ritual (toggles, key, tach needle, exhaust tip, then the whole car) builds anticipation for a sound payoff in 18 seconds with zero talking. 68x the account median but only 0.28 percent shares, so it won on rewatches and likes, not sends.
Who sends it, to whom: Hot rod and V8 guys to the buddy who loves a loud small block; mostly watched, rarely sent
Shape you can borrow alone: Hand-held sequence of the start-up ritual in close-ups (switch, key, gauge, tailpipe), then one wide shot of the truck running, one word at the end.

First 3 seconds: Tom stands on grass in front of the white Mustang holding a big polished stainless exhaust tip and starts talking straight to camera
Hook (said or on screen): "What's up? My name is Tom and I own Speedy's Equipment, the only provider of these super sexy NASCAR style boom tube exhaust tips."
Why it went viral: A product pitch that pays off with the sound: 12 seconds of talking, then he walks to the car and the rest is the exhaust note. Odd shiny object plus "sound like this" proof made an ad travel (31x median, 26.7k saves from shoppers).
Who sends it, to whom: Guys building a car to the friend who is picking exhaust; saved more than shared
Shape you can borrow alone: Hold the part in your hands, say what it is in two sentences, then cut to the truck doing the thing the part is for.

Why it went viral: Eight seconds of a pull through the gears with his reaction at the end (looks at camera, then yells). Pure sound and feel, loops easily, 20x median on a 0.53 percent share rate.
Who sends it, to whom: Manual truck guys to the buddy who misses his stick shift truck
Shape you can borrow alone: Phone clamped on the passenger side pointed at the driver, one pull through the gears, no talking, end on your face.

First 3 seconds: Same passenger-side angle in the Mustang, hand already on the shifter in a patch of sunlight, harness on, fields going by

Why it went viral: Nine seconds of relaxed shifting with a good exhaust note; it is a mood clip that loops. 16x median, modest 0.38 percent shares, so reach came from replays.
Who sends it, to whom: Stick shift people to each other, low intent
Shape you can borrow alone: Fixed cab cam on the shifter hand and the driver, one calm run through the gears, nothing said.

Who sends it, to whom: Buyers save it for themselves
Shape you can borrow alone: Open on a tight moving close-up of the part before your face ever appears, then 20 seconds of what it is.

Why it went viral: Five-second milestone clip: a known project car moves under its own power for the first time. Short enough to loop several times; followers who knew the build carried it (0.12 percent shares, only 85 comments).

First 3 seconds: A guy in a striped beanie and Dr Pepper shirt kneels at the side of a car running a polisher on the paint; Snapchat-style caption bar across the middle
Hook (said or on screen): On-screen text: "TF is my detailer doing?"
Why it went viral: Caught-on-camera gag: the detailer drifts off the panel, the spinning polisher ends up on his own leg and he reacts out loud. It reads like a candid of a coworker being a goof, which is why it has 6.36 percent shares, more than six times the next best post on the account, on only 12x median views.
Who sends it, to whom: Anyone who works in a shop to the coworker who does dumb stuff: "this is you"
Shape you can borrow alone: Caption bar that blames an unseen helper or "the new guy" over a clip of yourself doing the job wrong, phone propped as if someone caught you.

First 3 seconds: Tom close to camera in a dirty shop shirt asking a question, then a cut to the rear quarter of the blue Mustang with "#1: NOISE COMPLAINT" on screen
Hook (said or on screen): "Which one of my currently running vehicles do you think sounds the best?"
Why it went viral: A numbered sound-off: one question, then each vehicle cold starts in turn with a label, so viewers stay to hear all of them and vote. Highest comment count in his set (1,862) because the format asks for a pick.
Who sends it, to whom: Car guys to a buddy to argue over which one wins
Shape you can borrow alone: Ask one "which is best" question to camera, then numbered clips of each truck or engine sound, answer held for the caption.

First 3 seconds: Empty two-lane road shot from the shoulder; a small white car appears far off and grows fast
Hook (said or on screen): No speech and no text; just the car approaching and the fly-by sound
Why it went viral: Seven-second fly-by: quiet road, then the Mustang rips past the camera. Anticipation plus the pass loops well (10.7x median), low sends at 0.22 percent.
Who sends it, to whom: Mustang and V8 fans, mostly likes
Shape you can borrow alone: Phone on the ground at the road edge, drive past it once, keep the whole approach in the clip.

First 3 seconds: Wide shot of a rusty patina 60s Mustang sitting in the rain, then a cut to a Honda badge in the grille and a red DOHC VTEC valve cover under the hood
Hook (said or on screen): No speech; the reveal is the Honda H badge and the VTEC engine in a Mustang
Why it went viral: The car is the hook: a rat-rod Mustang with a turbo Honda engine is a "wait, what" build that splits Ford and Honda people. Eight seconds of quick detail cuts; best share rate of his non-skit posts at 0.99 percent.
Who sends it, to whom: Ford guys to Honda guys and back, as a dare or a laugh
Shape you can borrow alone: Eight seconds of quick detail cuts on the one thing about the truck people would not expect, wide shot first, the surprise by second two.

First 3 seconds: Dave outside in the lot points left at a white GMC, then swings his arm right toward a red GMC in the bay; camera follows his arm
Hook (said or on screen): "This beautiful truck and that beautiful truck have the exact same problem, and that one cost 10 times more to fix than that one, and I'm gonna tell you why."
Why it went viral: Two matching trucks, same mistake (DEF in the fuel tank), one bill ten times the other, with the physical proof (crystals, torn-down pump) and one rule: do not turn the key. Money stakes plus a mistake any diesel owner can make at the pump; 36x median, 24.7k shares.
Who sends it, to whom: Diesel owners to family, employees and buddies who drive diesels: "if you ever do this, do not start it"
Shape you can borrow alone: Point at two things that look the same, state the cost gap in the first sentence, show the evidence, end on one rule.

First 3 seconds: Dave leaning on the fender of a Ram 2500 with the hood up, talking, then the camera pans across the truck and the Cummins badge
Hook (said or on screen): "Never heard this problem. This is gonna be a new one for me. Cummins that just free spins."
Why it went viral: A veteran admits he is stumped, lets you hear the engine crank, lists what has been ruled out, then asks everyone to guess before teardown. 3,704 comments on 0.09 percent shares: a comment-driven mystery, it spread on arguments not sends.
Who sends it, to whom: Cummins owners and techs comment their diagnosis; few send it
Shape you can borrow alone: State a problem you have not solved, play the sound, list what you already checked, ask for guesses and promise the answer.

First 3 seconds: Full-screen macro of white frost-like crystals, camera pulling back slowly to show they fill a black pan
Hook (said or on screen): "Isn't this the most beautiful thing you've ever seen?"
Why it went viral: A strange, pretty texture you cannot identify, then the reveal that it is DEF left sitting three weeks, then he breaks it with his hand to show it is rock hard. Visual curiosity plus anger at emissions systems drove 54.6k shares (1.88 percent).
Who sends it, to whom: Diesel owners to every other diesel owner, and to the guy who defends DEF
Shape you can borrow alone: Open on a close-up of something from the shop nobody can identify, name it at second six, then touch or break it on camera.

First 3 seconds: Dave leaning over a front end talking to camera with a tech beside him; no visual change for the first 30 seconds
Hook (said or on screen): "I want to show you something, especially because it's summertime and it's getting hot."
Why it went viral: A seasonal problem everyone has (AC not cold) with a free check anyone can do: a radiator and condenser packed with debris. Highest saves in his set (84.5k) and 66.9k shares at 2.39 percent, because it is useful to people who do not turn wrenches and it posted July 1.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck owners to a spouse, parent or buddy whose AC is weak; techs to other techs
Shape you can borrow alone: Name a seasonal complaint, say what other shops get wrong, then show the simple thing to look at yourself.

First 3 seconds: A young tech in ear protection sets a bare 7.3 block on a stand, then close-ups of gloved hands working
Hook (said or on screen): No speech; a silent build montage (caption: "7.3 Ford Power Stroke Engine Build with Bob the Builder")
Why it went viral: Nearly two minutes of clean hands-on assembly of a 7.3 Power Stroke, piece by piece, with no talking. Satisfying process footage holds watch time (19x median) but nobody sends it (0.11 percent).
Who sends it, to whom: 7.3 fans watch to the end; little sharing
Shape you can borrow alone: Silent time-ordered montage of one job from bare part to finished, tight shots of hands, no voice.

First 3 seconds: Dave leaning on an engine talking to camera, then a cut to a selfie clip of a mom and dad, then their 17-year-old with his 7.3 on a stand
Hook (said or on screen): "Apparently, the rumors are there's some young man that's trying to do a 7.3 for himself in a truck."
Why it went viral: A feel-good story about a 17-year-old rebuilding his first engine, stitched from the family's own video, ending with Dave asking the audience whether he should help. 9,042 comments, the most in his set, but only 827 shares: people voted in the comments.
Who sends it, to whom: Viewers comment and tag; rarely sent
Shape you can borrow alone: React to a clip or message a follower sent you, say why it got to you, and ask the audience what you should do about it.

First 3 seconds: Dave standing in the shop with a tech beside him holding a tablet scan tool; cut to the tool's screen
Hook (said or on screen): "Mucar makes a really good scan tool."
Why it went viral: Sponsored scan tool demo with a discount code. 2.0M views against 24.3k likes and 0.04 percent shares does not look like organic spread; possibly promoted, but unclear. Do not read the view count as proof the format works.
Who sends it, to whom: Nobody, in practice
Shape you can borrow alone: Nothing to borrow as a viral shape; if a tool is shown, show it finding a real fault on a real truck.

First 3 seconds: Dave close to camera holding up fingers and counting, then a cut to techs loading plates at a catered lunch table
Hook (said or on screen): "There's five things I do in my shop to make my team's life more exciting and comfortable here in the shop."
Why it went viral: A boss listing concrete perks (payday lunch, prize wheel, snacks, chiropractor, bidets) with footage of each and a funny last item. People send it at their own boss or share it as "this is how you run a shop": 32.5k shares, 2.32 percent, 205k likes on 1.4M views.
Who sends it, to whom: Techs to coworkers and bosses: "must be nice"; shop owners to each other
Shape you can borrow alone: Count a short list on your fingers to camera, one concrete item per cut, save the oddest one for last.

First 3 seconds: Dave leaning over the same Ram's engine bay with a tech behind him, talking to camera
Hook (said or on screen): "We found the problem because of you guys. Isn't that a wonderful thing?"
Why it went viral: The answer video to the free-spinning Cummins mystery: he credits commenters who called a stuck throttle plate, then the truck starts on camera. Payoff for people who guessed (12x median), smaller than the question video, 0.21 percent shares.
Who sends it, to whom: People who commented on part one; Cummins owners save the fix
Shape you can borrow alone: Part two that opens by crediting the audience's answer, shows the fix, and ends on the engine starting.

First 3 seconds: Dave close to camera in the machine shop, a news headline card about a GM recall pops up at second two
Hook (said or on screen): "This motor has cost GM over $1 billion."
Why it went viral: Big-number hook on a current recall, then he holds the actual crank and bearing and explains the cause with measurements and an ocean-wave analogy. News timing and a brand fight drove 2,019 comments; 0.44 percent shares over 111 seconds.
Who sends it, to whom: GM owners to other GM owners; Ford and Ram guys to the GM buddy as a jab
Shape you can borrow alone: Open with one dollar figure about a known problem, hold the failed part in your hand, explain the cause with one everyday comparison.

First 3 seconds: He stands in front of a silver Ram holding a huge polished fan-shaped exhaust tip against his chest, white text box on top, then a quick cut to him crouched holding it up to the rear bumper.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Putting BOOM TUBES On My Diesel Truck". Spoken: "I'm putting boom tubes on my diesel truck."
Why it went viral: 182x his median but only 0.08 percent shares, so this was pushed by watch time and a live trend, not by sends: an odd shiny object in frame at second zero, a trend borrowed from car TikTok (stitched clip of the car creator), and a claim to be first on a diesel. It never delivers the sound (turbo is dead), which kept people watching and arguing in comments.
Who sends it, to whom: Barely shared. The few sends are truck guys to a buddy with "look what they are doing now".
Shape you can borrow alone: Hold the strange part in frame from the first frame, say in one line what you are about to do with it, explain what it is, and end on an open promise of the result.

First 3 seconds: Split screen: top half is footage of a well-known truck YouTuber being walked in handcuffs by an officer, bottom half is Zac's face close to a small fuzzy mic, text box across the middle.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Whistlindiesel Has Been Arrested For Tax Evasion". Spoken: "WhistlinDiesel has been arrested for tax evasion."
Why it went viral: 45x median. He was early on breaking news about the biggest name in the truck world, and the arrest footage is on screen the whole time while he explains the Montana plate angle in plain words. Shares are modest (0.34 percent); it rode search and curiosity.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck and car guys to the group chat: "did you see this".
Shape you can borrow alone: News desk: the source clip on the top half, your face and a mic on the bottom half, headline as the first sentence, then what happened and what it means for a regular owner, in 60 seconds.

First 3 seconds: POV hands shake a green spray can and point it at the license plate on a Super Duty bumper, then hold the can label up to the lens.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Protecting My License Plate From Flock Cameras". Spoken: "I'm going to show you how to protect the license plate on your truck from Flock cameras using this."
Why it went viral: 43x median with 36,500 shares (1.59 percent). A cheap hardware-store can aimed at a thing a lot of drivers resent (plate reader cameras), plus scarcity: "get it before they stop selling it" and the store clerk story at the end. The topic reaches far past truck people.
Who sends it, to whom: Anyone who distrusts the cameras, to friends and family who drive: "go get a can".
Shape you can borrow alone: One cheap off-the-shelf product, shown in hand in the first second, solving a thing drivers are annoyed by, with the exact product name said out loud. Skip the plate trick itself: covering or altering a plate is illegal in most states.

First 3 seconds: He crouches at the back of a lifted Super Duty and points at a giant flat exhaust tip sticking out under the bumper, text box on top, then cuts to him walking up holding the part.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "How To Install BOOM TUBES". Spoken: "We finally have the boom tubes on the truck."
Why it went viral: 30x median, 0.05 percent shares. It is the payoff episode to the 9.8M video, so the audience was already waiting, and the result looks ridiculous on purpose. Views came from the series and comments, not sends.
Who sends it, to whom: Almost nobody shares it. It is a follow-along for people who saw part one.
Shape you can borrow alone: Part two of a promise: open on the finished thing already on the truck, then rewind and show the install in quick POV steps.

First 3 seconds: He stands next to a silver Ram holding a long white PVC pipe upright like a staff and points at it, text box on top, then a clip of another creator's truck with PVC bars.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Making PVC Traction Bars". Spoken: "Thanks to PVC traction bars." (shouts out the guy who did it first, "this is going to save me a bunch of money")
Why it went viral: 26x median. A deliberately dumb budget build played completely straight: a 70 dollar PVC copy of a part that costs many hundreds. Half the viewers laugh, half get mad and comment that it does nothing, and both groups feed it.
Who sends it, to whom: Truck guys to the buddy who overspends on parts, or to the buddy who would actually do this.
Shape you can borrow alone: Build the cheap fake version of an expensive part with a straight face, step by step in POV, and end on the price.

First 3 seconds: He crouches at the hitch of a Ram holding a bag of zip ties, a red tow strap lying on the ground, text box on top.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Diesel Truck vs Zipties". Spoken: "How many zip ties does it take to stop my truck?"
Why it went viral: 26x median but 0.02 percent shares. A pure curiosity test with a counting ladder (1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75) and a visible snap each round, so people stay to see the number where it holds. Watch time carried it; nobody sends it.
Who sends it, to whom: Hardly anyone. It is a watch-to-the-end video, not a send.
Shape you can borrow alone: One question in the first sentence, then an escalating count with the same locked-off camera angle each round, so the only thing that changes is the number.

First 3 seconds: Top half: a truck rolling coal on a road. Bottom half: his face close to a mic. Text box across the middle. At 3 seconds it cuts to a White House press clip.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "ITS LEGAL TO DELETE DIESELS AGAIN (With Proof)". Spoken: "Breaking news. The Clean Air Act will no longer be enforced."
Why it went viral: 22x median with 29,700 shares (2.48 percent). It tells diesel owners the thing they most want to hear and shows official footage as proof. Note the claim is overstated (dropping criminal cases is not the same as deleting being legal), and that overstatement is a big part of why it traveled.
Who sends it, to whom: Every diesel owner to every other diesel owner, and to the buddy who got fined or is scared to delete.
Shape you can borrow alone: Good-news-for-owners bulletin: the official clip first, then your face saying what changed and what did not, in plain words. Jacob can be the one who gets it right.

First 3 seconds: He is lying on his side on the driveway under a silver Ram wrestling an orange traction bar, text box on top, then a close shot of fresh drilled holes in the frame.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Traction Bar Install DIDN'T End Well". Spoken: "I don't know how, but I found a way to mess up a bolt-on installation."
Why it went viral: 18x median, 0.03 percent shares. He admits the failure up front and asks for help in the caption, which pulls a flood of advice and roasting comments. It also calls back to the PVC bars. Comment bait through honesty, not a send.
Who sends it, to whom: Rarely shared. People comment instead: the ones who know how to set a rivnut.
Shape you can borrow alone: Open with the mistake already made and shown on camera, rewind through how it happened, end on the real question you need answered.

First 3 seconds: A photo of a two-tone brown and tan Ford Taurus fills the top, his cut-out face in a bucket hat talks in the lower corner on black, text box on top.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "King Ranch Taurus is Straight Aura". Spoken: "I've seen a King Ranch F250, but have you seen a King Ranch Ford Taurus?"
Why it went viral: 17x median with 25,000 shares (2.81 percent, his best send rate). An odd find everyone can judge in one second, compared side by side with the truck it copies, and it ends on a simple yes or no question.
Who sends it, to whom: Ford guys to each other, and to the buddy with a King Ranch: "you need the matching car".
Shape you can borrow alone: React to one weird vehicle photo: "you have seen X, but have you seen Y", show the photo, compare it to the truck people know, ask would you buy it.

First 3 seconds: Top half: a graphic of three diesel engines under "R.I.P." (6.7 Cummins, L5P Duramax, Power Stroke). Bottom half: his face at a mic. Then engine bay photos swap in as he names each one.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "2027 Is The End of a Era For Modern Diesels". Spoken: "2027 will be the end of an era for modern-day diesels as we know it."
Why it went viral: 16x median with 17,200 shares (1.94 percent). An end-of-an-era headline that covers all three brands, so every camp has a stake, with spec numbers on screen for each. The claims are thinly sourced, which also drives arguing in comments.
Who sends it, to whom: Brand loyalists to their rival-brand buddy, and owners to the buddy about to buy a new truck.
Shape you can borrow alone: Three-brand rundown: one big claim, then Ford, Ram and GM each get 15 seconds with a photo and two numbers on screen. Only with numbers he can back up.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle selfie by an open truck door, bearded guy talking to himself about putting on a hoodie, small text box on top. At 3 seconds it cuts to the same guy in red wraparound shades as a second character.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Carhartt gatekeepers be like". Spoken: "Getting chilly out, better grab the Carhartt sweater." / "Carhartt? He must have served. Where were you deployed?"
Why it went viral: 23x median. A two-character skit that names a brand nearly everyone owns and a guy everyone has met, pushed to absurd (stolen valor for a hoodie). People tag whoever wears Carhartt without doing trade work.
Who sends it, to whom: Tradesmen to the office friend in a Carhartt, and the office friend back to the tradesman.
Shape you can borrow alone: One man, two characters: normal guy says an innocent line, cut to the same man in sunglasses overreacting. Same low angle, sunglasses are the whole costume.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle indoor selfie, bald bearded guy says his salary to the room. At 3 seconds it cuts to him in purple shield glasses facing the other way.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Welders for no reason". Spoken: "You know, I didn't do too bad this year. I made about 85,000." / "85,000? What's it like living below the poverty line, cupcake?"
Why it went viral: 22x median. It roasts one specific trade for bragging about money and the truck, with quotable insults ("cupcake", "don't even fill up the Duramax"). Everyone knows that welder.
Who sends it, to whom: Every trade to the welder they know, and welders to each other.
Shape you can borrow alone: "[Group] for no reason" title, then the calm guy states a normal fact and the sunglasses character one-ups it until it gets ridiculous.

First 3 seconds: Outdoor low-angle selfie in falling snow, guy in a gray beanie looks up and remarks on the weather. At 3 seconds, same guy in pink shades answers.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When you complain about the weather around a blue collar guy". Spoken: "Geez, this weather sure is nasty." / "Try working in it, buddy. 168 hour shifts. You'd fold like a lawn chair."
Why it went viral: 22x median. A universal small-talk moment met with a line every outdoor worker has said or heard, and posted while it was actually snowing. The "168 hours" bit is his running joke.
Who sends it, to whom: Wives and coworkers to the blue collar guy who says exactly this, and tradesmen to each other.
Shape you can borrow alone: Take one everyday sentence people say to you and answer it as the over-the-top tough guy, filmed outside in the actual weather.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle indoor selfie, bald bearded guy asks about base model trucks. At 4 seconds he cuts to himself in dark shades as the salesman.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Buying a truck in 2025 be like". Spoken: "What do you guys have for base models? You know, just cloth interior, nothing fancy."
Why it went viral: 20x median but a low 0.15 percent shares. Truck prices are a sore spot for every buyer, and the 57,000 dollar base model line lands as the punch. It was watched and agreed with more than it was sent.
Who sends it, to whom: Guys shopping for a truck to the buddy who just bought one, or to dad: "this is why I am keeping the old one".
Shape you can borrow alone: Buyer and salesman, both played by him: a reasonable ask, then one real price delivered deadpan as the punchline.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle indoor selfie, guy stretches and says he has to get to bed. At 3 seconds, same guy in black shield shades cuts in.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Concrete guys be like". Spoken: "Geez, I better get to bed. I've got to be up at 5 a.m." / "Cupcake. I'm already on my fifth coffee by 5 a.m."
Why it went viral: 20x median. Trade-specific bragging (up earlier, works alone, Duramax lit up like a stadium) that ends with the truck not being paid off. The roasted trade shares it proudly.
Who sends it, to whom: Concrete guys to their crew, and other trades to the concrete guy they know.
Shape you can borrow alone: "[Trade] guys be like": the normal guy sets up with a plain line, the character tops it three times, and the last line undercuts him.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle indoor selfie, guy in dark shades already mid-complaint. Text box on top. At 5 seconds the calm version of him answers.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Blue collar finances". Spoken: "I mean, I'm working 168 hours a day and I barely have enough money to eat." / "I thought you make like 45 bucks an hour."
Why it went viral: 19x median. The truck payment joke: good wage, broke anyway because of an 1,100 dollar Duramax payment, Zyns, energy drinks, a boat and a side-by-side. It stings because it is true for a lot of viewers.
Who sends it, to whom: Wives and girlfriends to the guy with the truck payment, and buddies to the one with the newest truck.
Shape you can borrow alone: Calm guy asks simple money questions, the character lists his expenses one short item at a time, each one worse.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle indoor shot of him looking into an open shoebox with new sneakers. At 3 seconds, same guy in orange shades cuts in.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Blue collar guys for no reason". Spoken: "Oh yeah, new pair of Jordans, these things are clean." / "Flexin' a 100 dollar pair of Jordans, cupcake. My work boots start at 500."
Why it went viral: 19x median with 54,200 shares. A prop in the first second and a familiar one-upper: whatever you bought, his work gear cost more and gets destroyed faster. Ends on the gas truck dig.
Who sends it, to whom: Friends and partners to the tradesman who turns everything into how hard he works.
Shape you can borrow alone: Start with a prop in hand and one happy line, then the character turns it into a contest about work.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle outdoor selfie under a porch roof, bald bearded guy politely asks to renew his license. At 3 seconds, same guy in blue mirrored shades as the clerk.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "DMV employees be like". Spoken: "I was just wondering if I could renew my driver's license, please." / "Do you have an original copy of the Treaty of Versailles, Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights?"
Why it went viral: 18x median with 70,100 shares (1.52 percent). Not a trades joke at all: everybody has been through the DMV, so the audience is the whole country, and the document list escalates to an umbilical cord.
Who sends it, to whom: Anyone to anyone who just went to the DMV, especially family.
Shape you can borrow alone: Pick a counter everyone has stood at, play the customer straight and the clerk asking for more and more absurd things.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle outdoor selfie against a cloudy sky, guy in a tan Carhartt cap as the boss starts an interview. At 5 seconds, same guy without the cap answers.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Blue collar interview (concrete version)". Spoken: "The job is just concrete laborer, so just tell me a little about yourself and why I should hire you."
Why it went viral: 17x median. A job interview turned upside down: every red flag (three divorces, child support, Duramax payment, lives at the Motel 6) makes him "overqualified". Crews recognize the guy.
Who sends it, to whom: Crew members to the boss and to each other: "this is our new hire".
Shape you can borrow alone: Interview format with a hat as the only costume change: the boss asks a normal question, the applicant answers with flaws that the boss treats as strengths.

First 3 seconds: Low-angle outdoor selfie under a bright blue sky, guy tilts his head back and says it is hot. At 2 seconds, same guy in red shield shades leans in.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When you mention the weather around a blue collar guy". Spoken: "It is hot out, my goodness." / "Why don't you try working in it, brother. 168 hours a week."
Why it went viral: 16x median but his best send rate: 107,800 shares (2.63 percent). It is the summer remake of the snow skit, posted in a heat wave, with a fresh bit (hot Gatorade, no time to collect ice). Proof that a working premise can be reshot by season.
Who sends it, to whom: Partners and office coworkers to the outdoor worker, and tradesmen to their crew in the heat.
Shape you can borrow alone: Reshoot a skit that already worked with one variable changed (season, weather, place), same title pattern and same character.

First 3 seconds: Phone sits on a gas station counter as the cashier's view. A big man in a red shirt and belt buckle struts up to the register asking for five on diesel, and a hard hat in a hi-vis vest steps in behind him.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When a trade worker runs into a trucker". Spoken: "What's up, Joe? ... You doing 1,800 miles today?"
Why it went viral: 56x the account median and the only one of his top ten with a real share rate (0.78 percent, about 10x his other hits). It picks a fight between two tribes ("trucking ain't a trade") so both sides send it and argue in the comments, and 63 seconds of escalating insults (clean vest, soft hands) keeps them watching.
Who sends it, to whom: Truckers to the union or trades buddy who talks down on driving, and trades guys back to their trucker friends
Shape you can borrow alone: State one side of an old truck-world argument straight to the camera as if the viewer just said the other side, and escalate the insults for 30 seconds.

First 3 seconds: Cashier point of view. A man in a grey Carhartt tee sets a foam box and a stack of sauce cups on the counter and opens the box to show one piece of chicken.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Customers when you charge for sauce". Spoken: "Hey, man, I just got one piece of chicken. That's it. $1.29."
Why it went viral: 32x median on views but only 0.04 percent shares, so this is watch-time and comment fuel, not send fuel. Everyone has been charged for sauce, and the customer's rising outrage ("Chick-fil-A says my pleasure") plays as a one-take argument people watch to the end.
Who sends it, to whom: Mostly not shared. A few send it to the friend who hoards sauce or fights every small charge
Shape you can borrow alone: Play one stubborn customer arguing a tiny charge to an unseen clerk, camera set where the clerk would stand.

First 3 seconds: Cashier point of view. Man in a dark Carhartt tee puts a big foam box on the counter and keeps his hand flat on the lid.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When the customer lies about their order". Spoken: "I just got a one-piece chicken tender and a piece of white toast."
Why it went viral: 28x median. The hand on the lid sets up a reveal in the first two seconds, so viewers stay 40 seconds to see the box opened (six pieces, then he blames the cook). Shares are low (0.07 percent), it is a retention piece.
Who sends it, to whom: Gas station and food counter workers to coworkers, "this is every day"
Shape you can borrow alone: Open with a closed box or covered thing you refuse to open, stall with excuses, then show it and blame someone else.

First 3 seconds: Cashier point of view. Same man sets two stacked foam boxes on the counter and says it is just toast and fries.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "How customers lie about their order". Spoken: "I got just a piece of toast and an order of fries in there."
Why it went viral: 27x median. It is the same closed-box reveal as his number 3 hit run again four months later, which shows the format is the engine, not the single joke. 0.05 percent shares, so watch time carried it.
Who sends it, to whom: Counter and restaurant workers to coworkers
Shape you can borrow alone: Repeat a proven bit with one detail changed (bigger box, bigger lie) and treat it as a series.

First 3 seconds: Cashier point of view. Man in a dark long sleeve walks up holding a foam cup, sets it on the counter and points at the camera.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Regulars when they see a new cashier". Spoken: "How you doing, sir. So buddy, new here?"
Why it went viral: 24x median. The entitled 15-year regular who has "never paid for a pop" is a character every small-town store and shop knows, and he lectures the new kid for a full minute. 0.04 percent shares, strong completion.
Who sends it, to whom: Small-town clerks and counter guys to coworkers, "this is so-and-so"
Shape you can borrow alone: Play the regular who expects the old deal and lectures the new guy, spoken straight to the lens.

First 3 seconds: Phone on a dispatch desk. A dispatcher types at two monitors showing a load map while two truckers in company shirts lean on the counter.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV- Truckers negotiating loads". Spoken: "Every time I ring the bell add 500."
Why it went viral: 22x median with a slightly better share rate (0.12 percent) because it is inside-trucking humor: two drivers bidding miles against each other while the dispatcher gets squeezed. It needs three people and a real office, and the setting is doing a lot of the work.
Who sends it, to whom: Truckers to their dispatcher, and dispatchers to their drivers
Shape you can borrow alone: Not a solo shape as shot. The solo version is one man haggling a rate out loud with a voice on the phone.

First 3 seconds: Backyard patio. A pressure washer is spraying siding while the customer walks into the spray line waving his arms to stop him, then turns to the camera.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "When you tell the contractor you're paying cash". Spoken: "How much is it gonna be?" then "I'm gonna pay with cash."
Why it went viral: 21x median. One word (cash) flips the whole mood and the price, which every tradesman and every customer recognizes instantly. 0.12 percent shares, so recognition more than sending.
Who sends it, to whom: Contractors and side-work guys to each other, and customers to their handyman
Shape you can borrow alone: Show the before and after of one magic word: the quote in a normal voice, then the same quote after hearing cash.

First 3 seconds: Wide shot of a black Ram in a parking lot, then a cut to a man in a hard hat and hi-vis vest eating a hot dog in the driver's seat as someone walks up to his window.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "You can't get a trade worker off break". Spoken: "Jojo, hey, I need to cut your break a little short."
Why it went viral: 18x median and his best share rate among the non-trade-war skits (0.14 percent). Break time is sacred on every crew, and a man in a truck cab refusing to put the hot dog down even after being fired is the fantasy version of what they all want to say.
Who sends it, to whom: Crew guys to the group chat and to the foreman who interrupts lunch
Shape you can borrow alone: Sit in the truck cab mid-lunch, treat the camera as the boss at the window, and refuse to move.

First 3 seconds: Shot from behind a hot food case full of fried chicken. A man in a white tee walks up, points at the food and leans over the glass.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Customers that come in at closing for a deal". Spoken: "What time y'all close? ... You want to run a deal on that?"
Why it went viral: 16x median. The closing-time haggler is another character every counter worker knows, and the camera angle behind the food makes the viewer the clerk. Low shares (0.06 percent), carried by watch time and comments.
Who sends it, to whom: Food counter and convenience store workers to coworkers
Shape you can borrow alone: Play the guy who shows up at closing wanting a deal, camera placed behind the thing he is trying to get cheap.

First 3 seconds: Wide shot of a gas station aisle. A man in a grey tee dances toward the register waving a five dollar bill over his head, grinning.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Diesel customers at the gas station". Spoken: "You heard the big news, brother? ... Give me five on that diesel, but not that regular diesel. Give me that red dye."
Why it went viral: 15x median with his second best share rate (0.43 percent). It rides a diesel news rumor (the character claims red dye off-road fuel is legal now) and plays the guy who was running it anyway, so diesel owners send it as both a joke and a "did you hear this".
Who sends it, to whom: Diesel truck owners to the buddy who runs or jokes about running red dye
Shape you can borrow alone: Walk in celebrating a piece of diesel news as a character who takes it one step too far, opening on movement instead of a standing start.

First 3 seconds: A monkey face cutout with eyes closed, slowly lifting its chin, pasted over a dark truck cab interior at night. White caption box sits above it the whole time.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: leaving for work in the dark while everyone else is snug as a bug in a rug". Audio is a sad song lyric.
Why it went viral: 908x the account median and 3.51 percent shares on a 9 second clip. The dark truck cab before sunrise is a feeling every early-shift worker has had alone, and the sad music plus a proud, tired face says it without a word spoken.
Who sends it, to whom: Early-shift workers to their wife or girlfriend still in bed, and to the crew chat
Shape you can borrow alone: One static shot of his own tired face in the dark cab before work, one line of text above, sad sound, under 10 seconds.

First 3 seconds: Macho Man Randy Savage cutout in a neon hat pulls off his sunglasses and leans bug-eyed into the lens, pasted over a jobsite photo.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: that one coworker at 6:30am". Audio: "I'm jacked up on 10,000 milligrams of caffeine"
Why it went viral: 436x median and the highest share rate in this batch (4.73 percent). "That one coworker" is a tag-a-friend prompt in disguise: every crew has the guy on three energy drinks at dawn, so people send it straight to him.
Who sends it, to whom: Crew members to the wired morning coworker, or to the chat with his name
Shape you can borrow alone: "That one guy at [early hour]" text over himself acting it out in the cab or lip-syncing a known wild sound clip.

First 3 seconds: Conor McGregor cutout struts toward the camera, arms swinging, over a photo of a house under construction. Two lines of text sit at the top.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "(Work starts at 7am) That one guy at 6:15:"
Why it went viral: 400x median but the lowest share rate of the account's top five (1.31 percent). Same "that one guy" early-bird idea as number 2 with a weaker clip, so it got views from the strut and fewer sends.
Who sends it, to whom: Crew members to the guy who always shows up 45 minutes early
Shape you can borrow alone: Two-line text setup (the rule, then "that one guy") over himself pulling in or walking up far too early.

First 3 seconds: A heavyset man in a white shirt and cap is mid-rant, lunging forward while a security guard holds him back, pasted over a jobsite photo.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: the real you slips out at work after that one coworker says the wrong thing"
Why it went viral: 234x median, 3.76 percent shares. Holding your temper at work until one coworker pushes it is universal, and the clip is a full meltdown. The joke is about temper and not race, but the audio is a rant full of the n-word, so the sound itself is not something Jacob should reuse.
Who sends it, to whom: Workers to the coworker who pushes their buttons, or to a friend who knows about him
Shape you can borrow alone: "The real you slips out when..." text over his own face going from calm to done, no borrowed audio.

First 3 seconds: John C. Reilly in a tuxedo from the Step Brothers job interview scene talks to the camera, cut with Will Ferrell, pasted over a construction site photo.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: the kind of employees my company hires". Audio: "I am no good before 11 a.m."
Why it went viral: 222x median, 4.48 percent shares. It lets workers complain about the useless new hire without naming anyone, and the movie scene is already loved, so the text only has to aim it at work.
Who sends it, to whom: Workers to the crew chat about the new hire, and to the boss as a jab
Shape you can borrow alone: A deadpan list of ridiculous limitations spoken to the camera as the worst new hire, under one line of text.

First 3 seconds: Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels from Dumb and Dumber stand side by side on a gravel lot. Labels read Coworker and Me, and Me points off into the distance.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Boss: who wants to come in on Saturday?" with labels "Coworker:" and "Me:"
Why it went viral: 170x median, 4.33 percent shares in 8 seconds. Dodging Saturday work is shared by every hourly worker, and the Boss, Coworker, Me labels make the joke readable in one second with the sound off.
Who sends it, to whom: Workers to the coworker who always says yes to Saturday, and to the boss
Shape you can borrow alone: Boss line as text, then his own reaction shot labeled Me (pointing away, already leaving).

First 3 seconds: A young man in glasses and a black tee walks into frame in an unfinished drywall room, looks up at the ceiling and his jaw drops as the camera pushes in.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: coming into work on Monday and remembering all of Fridays "Monday problems"". Audio: "oh f, oh my god"
Why it went viral: 131x median, 3.35 percent shares. "That's a Monday problem" is a phrase people in shops and on sites actually say on Friday, so seeing the bill come due is instantly recognized. A real person's face on a real site worked as well as a celebrity cutout.
Who sends it, to whom: Coworkers to each other on Monday morning, and to whoever said "Monday problem" on Friday
Shape you can borrow alone: Walk into the shop or up to the truck, look at something off camera and let the face drop, with a shop-phrase caption.

First 3 seconds: Kurt Angle cutout in a white tee stares wide-eyed and unblinking into the lens over a house construction photo. Nothing else moves.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "POV: a group of kids walks by the jobsite and you hear "that's us if we don't lock in fr""
Why it went viral: 104x median, 3.78 percent shares on 7 seconds. Self-deprecating pride: tradesmen being used as the cautionary tale and staring back. The audience laughs at the insult because they recognize it.
Who sends it, to whom: Tradesmen to the crew chat, and to younger family members as a joke
Shape you can borrow alone: Overheard insult as the text, his own blank stare into the lens as the whole video.

First 3 seconds: Steve Carell cutout in a cardigan laughs and waves his hands as if telling a story, over a construction site photo. Two blocks of text carry the whole joke.
Hook (said or on screen): Text: "Hey why do you call the boss's son Rusty... that's not his name?" "Me: It stands for Rusty Rifle... he doesn't work, and he can't be fired"
Why it went viral: 81x median but only 0.84 percent shares, the weakest share rate of this account's top ten. It is a written joke (a pun on the boss's son) that you read once, not a feeling you recognize, and it risks landing on the wrong person if sent at work.
Who sends it, to whom: Workers at family-run shops to a trusted coworker, quietly
Shape you can borrow alone: Question and answer nickname joke in two text blocks over his own laugh. Lower priority, puns share worse than feelings here.
